theory: The coder's wrong first choices are its reading of the description: re-read with other examples it picks the same wrong program (SeedLM-25). Each training task is read in one wording only, so the coder learns which words go with which program for that wording. Reading every training task in several wordings should teach the meaning instead of the wording
data: 1,200 training tasks (the 525 real training tasks with engine programs, outputs/seedlm/v2/real_dev.json, and 675 training teacher tasks drawn at random), two paraphrases each written by three teacher subagents; a paraphrase is kept only if it differs from the original and from the other paraphrase and the literals the coder reads (numbers and quoted strings) are the same values in the same order (scripts/seedlm26_paraphrase_check.py). Teachers see only these descriptions and one visible example each
arms: for each base coder s12-a1, s12-a2, s12-a3: two fine-tunes from its checkpoint, 400 steps, the base run's data mix (a fresh synthetic draw of 60,000) plus rows of the same 1,200 tasks at a tenth of the mix: s26-o<k> with the original descriptions (each task twice, to match the count), s26-p<k> with the two paraphrases instead. Learning rates 0.3 of the base run's, 20-step warm-up, linear decay (scripts/seedlm26_finetune.py). Nothing else runs while they train
primary_measure: held-out teacher tasks (139): the first program at beam width 32 that reproduces the visible example is right on every case (SeedLM-15's cache), mean over the three bases of s26-p<k> minus s26-o<k>. Supported if at least +3; not supported if at most 0; inconclusive otherwise
secondary_measures: development fifth (94), each coder alone, the same difference
the held-out teacher tasks with terse, MBPP-like descriptions (SeedLM-8, data/seedlm/teacher_holdout_terse.json), the same difference
choice: diagnostic; the system's adoption rule is unchanged

outcome.primary: held-out teacher tasks, s26-p<k> minus s26-o<k>: +4 (62 vs 58), +6 (61 vs 55), -2 (56 vs 58); mean +2.67, between 0 and +3: inconclusive (reports/seedlm/paraphrase_compare.json)
secondary: development fifth, alone: 0 (59 vs 59), +3 (54 vs 51), +1 (57 vs 56); mean +1.33
terse held-out teacher descriptions: +3 (60 vs 57), -3 (54 vs 57), 0 (62 vs 62); mean 0 (reports/seedlm/terse_s26-*.json)
outcome.reported: against the base coders (teacher 59, 59, 62; development 56, 53, 58): the original-words arm fell to 58, 55, 58 and 59, 51, 56; the paraphrase arm held at 62, 61, 56 and 59, 54, 57
outcome.reading: Repeating 1,200 training tasks in their own words for 400 steps cost the coders about 3 held-out teacher tasks; repeating them in two other wordings did not. The gain over the control is mostly the harm it avoided: paraphrases worked as a guard against memorizing the wording, not as a new skill, and they did not make terse descriptions easier
outcome.choice: no new method; next: whether paraphrases delay the coder's 30-minute overfitting (SeedLM-27)
